name: Turmeric / gram flour hair removal paste

lead: Ubtan-style pastes are used at home to rub away fine body hair, slow its regrowth and leave skin looking brighter and smoother. Ubtan is a traditional herbal formulation from the Indian system of medicine, commonly made from gram (chickpea) flour and turmeric among other ingredients.

Proponents describe it as a gentle abrasive plant mixture that rubs fine hair away and, with repeated use, thins regrowth. A 2016 Journal of Ethnopharmacology study standardised ubtan as a skin-care preparation; no published study tested it for hair removal.

paras: People mix the flour and turmeric with a liquid into a paste, spread it on the skin, let it dry, then rub it off in the direction against the hair. It is repeated regularly and suits fine hair best.
No safety data specific to hair removal were found. Turmeric is known to stain skin and fabric, and topical plant preparations can in general cause irritation or allergic reactions.

chain: Fine hair loosens or regrows slower
angle.text: Home ubtan pastes of gram flour and turmeric are used to rub off fine body hair, slow regrowth and brighten the skin. Research has studied ubtan as a skin-care formulation, not as hair removal.

lead: A turmeric and gram flour paste is a traditional South Asian home preparation used to make fine facial and body hair less visible or easier to lift away, leaving smoother, brighter-looking skin. Gram flour (besan) is a flour made from split chickpeas, and turmeric is the yellow spice from Curcuma longa; mixed with a liquid they form a paste that is spread on the skin and rubbed off once dry.[1][2]

The paste is related to ubtan, a traditional herbal skin-care formulation of the Indian system of medicine, used for skin care across the Indian subcontinent and now also sold commercially under that name.[3] Turmeric paste is also applied to the bride and groom before weddings in many Hindu communities in a ritual called haldi.[2]

Practitioners say that with repeated use the paste lifts fine hair and slows regrowth. No published study has tested the paste for hair removal; the closest research is a 2016 laboratory study that prepared and standardised ubtan and evaluated it as a skin-care formulation.[3]

South Asian skin care; haldi ritual[2]

paras: Ubtan is a traditional herbal formulation used for skin care across the Indian subcontinent for a long time, and several commercial skin products carry the name.[3] The hair-removal variant mixes gram flour and turmeric into a paste that is applied to the area and rubbed off once dry; the practice is described here at a general level.

Gram flour is a gluten-free pulse flour from split chickpeas that is a staple of Indian cooking; Wikipedia's article on it covers culinary uses.[1] Wikipedia's article on turmeric describes its use in body painting in Austronesian and Micronesian cultures and the haldi pre-wedding ritual in Hindu communities.[2]
Practitioners of the folk method say the paste lifts fine hair and, with repeated use, reduces regrowth and brightens the skin. No published study has tested these claims.

Wikipedia notes that turmeric and curcumin have been studied mainly in low-quality clinical trials and describes a 2016 systematic review on turmeric and skin health among its references; its safety discussion concerns oral use.[2] Like other plant pastes, turmeric can stain skin, and any topical preparation can cause irritation or contact allergy in some people.

No studies found. The closest research is a 2016 laboratory study that prepared and standardised ubtan using chromatographic techniques and evaluated it as a skin-care formulation, not as a hair remover.[3]
